title: DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY WITH VARIABLE INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY AND DYSMORPHIC FACIES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental delay with variable intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies (DIDDF) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the JARID2 gene (601594) on chromosome 6p22.3.

checks.explanation: Haploinsufficiency implies heterozygous loss-of-function.

paragraphs.text: Developmental delay with variable intellectual disability and dysmorphic facies (DIDDF) is a neurodevelopmental syndrome caused by JARID2 haploinsufficiency (Verberne et al., 2021). It is characterized by developmental delay, cognitive impairment ranging from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, autistic features, and behavior abnormalities. Dysmorphic facial features include a high anterior hairline, broad forehead, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, and full lips (Verberne et al., 2022).

checks.claim: DIDDF is a neurodevelopmental syndrome caused by JARID2 haploinsufficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: We report that JARID2 haploinsufficiency leads to a clinically distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome
checks.explanation: The abstract directly states that JARID2 haploinsufficiency causes a neurodevelopmental syndrome. Using the name DIDDF for that syndrome is the entry's own naming.

paragraphs.text: Barøy et al. (2013) described 4 unrelated patients with de novo 6p22.3 deletions including JARID2: 2 females aged 15 and 6.5 years and 2 males aged 4 and 6.5 years. Three were of Norwegian or Norwegian/English ancestry and 1 was Lebanese, and all had nonconsanguineous parents. All 4 had developmental delay with cognitive impairment ranging from borderline IQ to severe intellectual disability. All had gait disturbance with impaired balance and coordination, and they shared similar facial dysmorphic features. These features included prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, dark infraorbital circles, midface hypoplasia, bulbous nasal tip, full lips, marked Cupid's bow, and a prominent or pointed chin. Other features were clinodactyly of the fifth fingers and foot anomalies such as syndactyly of toes. Two patients had seizures or seizure-suspected episodes, 3 had behavioral abnormalities, 1 had autism spectrum disorder, and 1 had an atrial septal defect.

paragraphs.text: The patient in the series of Barøy et al. (2013) with the smallest JARID2-containing deletion (Patient 4) was a 6.5-year-old Lebanese boy of nonconsanguineous parents. He walked at 16 months. At age 4 years 3 months his language delay was 1.5 years, and at 6.5 years his IQ was 74 (borderline). He had balance and coordination problems, poor finger opposition, and early-onset muscular hypotonia. Neuromuscular and metabolic workups were normal, as were cerebral MRI and EEG. He had the characteristic facial features, strabismus, fifth-finger clinodactyly, syndactyly of toes 2-3, sandal gap, and broad halluces.

paragraphs.text: Barøy et al. (2013) also reviewed 10 previously reported patients with deletions including JARID2. The characteristic facial features had not been consistently reported in these patients, but photographs were available for 7 of them and confirmed a similar facial pattern. Four of the 10 had impaired balance, impaired coordination, and/or gait disturbance. The authors suggested that JARID2 haploinsufficiency may result in a clinically recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome. They recommended sequencing JARID2 in similar patients who did not have a deletion.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) summarized 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants: 4 males and 4 females aged 5 to 36 years, 5 of whom had been reported previously. All 8 had developmental delay. Intellectual functioning ranged from normal (1 patient) through learning difficulties or borderline functioning to moderate intellectual disability. Four of the 8 had autistic features, including 2 with a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. Three had behavior abnormalities, 2 had hypotonia, and 2 had gait disturbance. Facial dysmorphism was variable. Additional anomalies included submucous cleft palate with bifid uvula, cryptorchidism, an arachnoid cyst or posterior fossa cyst/mega cisterna magna, kyphoscoliosis, and cafe-au-lait macules.

paragraphs.text: Barøy et al. (2013) performed aCGH in a cohort of about 3,600 patients ascertained for neurodevelopmental disorders and identified de novo 6p22.3-p24.1 deletions in 5 patients. The deletions in 4 of these patients ranged from 189 kb to 4.8 Mb and shared a smallest region of overlap (SRO I) of 189 kb that included JARID2 and DTNBP1. This region was defined by the 189-kb deletion in Patient 4, which removed exons 3 to 18 and the 3-prime UTR of JARID2 and exons 7 to 10 of DTNBP1. Parental testing showed that all deletions were de novo. The Database of Genomic Variants (DGV) contained only CNVs covering minor parts of the region.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) also tested 3 patients with JARID2 missense variants of uncertain significance against a DNA methylation episignature (see DIAGNOSIS). Two unrelated patients (9 and 11) carried c.2363G-A (p.Arg788Gln). In patient 11 this variant was inherited from an apparently unaffected mother. Patient 10 carried a de novo c.1930G-A (p.Glu644Lys) variant in the ARID domain. All 3 patients clustered with controls and had scores near zero. The authors noted that this did not rule out pathogenicity but suggested that the variants might be benign. Patients 9 and 10 lacked the typical facial dysmorphism, and patient 11 had severe global spasticity and lack of myelination.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) used EPIC arrays to analyze peripheral blood DNA methylation in 8 patients with pathogenic or likely pathogenic JARID2 variants and 56 matched controls. They identified a 150-probe episignature that clearly separated patients from controls on hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling, and the signature was confirmed by leave-one-out cross-validation. A support vector machine classifier gave all patients scores near 1. Controls and samples from 57 other disorders received low scores, which the authors interpreted as full sensitivity and specificity.
